name: Village Enterprise: poverty graduation in East Africa (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: shares of the result by branch at the defaults (households × first-year gain × evidence and missing-data steps): Uganda's core program, DREAMS and SPRINT 32%, Kenya 28%, Ethiopia's DREAMS camps 25%, Rwanda 12%, Tanzania's DREAMS 3%; the government-adoption row, under 1%, left out.
summary: Village Enterprise runs a one-year poverty graduation program for the poorest rural households in Uganda, Kenya, Rwanda, Ethiopia and Tanzania: business training, seed grants to groups of three entrepreneurs, mentoring and savings groups, a quarter of the households in DREAMS, its program for refugee settlements with Mercy Corps in Uganda and Ethiopia and through local organisations in Tanzania. Against its fiscal year 2025 spending (US$21.0M with overhead, 47,505 households), two randomized trials of the program itself (consumption 7.3% higher in Kenya, 3.6% in Uganda, 17% in DREAMS and 13% for its refugees, among all households offered the program) give about {{result}} years of healthy life per $1,000. The biggest uncertainty is how long the consumption gain lasts: the trials followed households for at most 2.5 years after the program, and the model assumes a gain fading 5% a year for 8 years (3 to 12). Tanzania's DREAMS households, the SPRINT digital pilot and governments' adoption of the model, which no trial has tested, are discounted for missing data.

rows.explainer: All of Village Enterprise's program spending in its fiscal year 2025 (July 2024 to June 2025, the latest audited year): Kenya $5.24M, Uganda $3.24M, Rwanda $1.50M, Ethiopia $1.67M, regional East Africa program staff $2.00M and US-booked program costs $3.42M (mostly the $2.32M subaward to Mercy Corps for DREAMS and $0.46M to IDinsight for the DREAMS evaluation, Form 990 Schedule I). Every program is a version of the same one-year poverty graduation model (training, seed grants to business groups of three, mentoring, savings groups), so all of it is counted against all the entrepreneurs it trained. That includes the refugee program DREAMS (32% of program spending, its own branch below), the nutrition-adapted program in northern Kenya (Nawiri, 6%, ended early in 2025), the work helping the Kenyan and Rwandan governments adopt the model (the Gates-funded county programme, US$827,441, Form 990 Schedule O), valued in uov_government_adoption, and two small activities with no reach of their own, savings-group technical help to the Wildlife Conservation Society's farmers and fishers in Madagascar and a one-year care-economy policy project with UN Women and West Pokot County (annual report pp. 12-13), valued in unmodelled_benefits_adj.

The report gives no FY2025 count: 1 to 3 staff-years in the two-district pilot at up to 600 businesses of three entrepreneurs each (1,800 per staff-year) gives 1,800 as the best guess (one staff-year), 600 to 5,400. rows.label: Yearly increase in ln(consumption), DREAMS Ethiopia (refugee camps)
rows.explainer: Ethiopia's DREAMS households are all refugees, in three camps in Dollo Ado, so they take the trial's refugee effect on participants (about 14%), not the all-household one. Its further doubt (Somali camps rather than South Sudanese settlements in Uganda) is in dreams_ethiopia_evidence_adj.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, DREAMS in Ethiopia's camps (internal and external validity)
rows.explainer: Internal validity of the trial (0.95, as core_evidence_adj) times its carry to Ethiopia (0.85). The Uganda trial's refugee effect carried to Ethiopia's Dollo Ado camps: arid, with less land for farming, a different refugee population (Somali) and tighter rules on refugees' work and movement than Uganda's settlements, but the same Village Enterprise program and grants. The carry is 0.85, a little deeper than the 0.92 core_evidence_adj makes for the core trial carried to new settings, because the population and setting differ more; 0.81 in all, 0.57 to 0.95.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, core program (Kenya, Uganda, Rwanda) (internal and external validity)
rows.explainer: Internal validity, about 0.95: two independent, pre-registered randomized trials of this program itself (and a third, IPA's in Uganda, with the same consumption effect), large samples, disbursement verified; consumption is self-reported, and the impact-bond trial's outcome paid the charity, which may have raised delivery quality during the trial. External validity, about 0.92: the FY2025 core program is wider than the trial (northern Kenya's drylands, Rwanda's government-linked delivery; the SPRINT digital pilot is its own branch), against which the trial ran partly during COVID-19 lockdowns (which lowered its Ugandan effects). 0.87, 0.7 to 1. Anchor: the site's GiveDirectly model takes recipients' consumption gains from its trials at face value (1) and cuts the weaker spillover evidence to 0.6 × 0.8; this program's trials are as strong as GiveDirectly's for recipients but measure a smaller effect, of a program that has since changed more.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, DREAMS Uganda (internal validity)
rows.explainer: DREAMS Uganda is the trial's own program in the trial's own settlements (later cohorts than those studied), so only the internal-validity part of core_evidence_adj (0.95): self-reported consumption, a household-level design in which some controls joined savings groups.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, DREAMS Tanzania (internal and external validity)
rows.explainer: The DREAMS trial's all-household effect carried to Tanzania, where local community-based organisations deliver DREAMS after Village Enterprise trains them, for naturalised former refugees and their neighbours: a new setting and delivery channel, so the same cut as core_evidence_adj (0.95 × 0.92), 0.7 to 1.

rows.label: Yearly fade of the consumption gain
rows.explainer: The program's own evidence shows no detectable fade over 0.5 to 2.5 years: across the core trial's seven cohorts there are no significant differences in consumption effects except the COVID-hit Cohort 4 (report printed p. 20, PDF p. 22). Inside that, Kenya's later cohorts (surveyed sooner after the program) had larger effects than earlier ones, a hint of fade, and Uganda's the reverse (the report finds the evidence for its lockdown explanation of Uganda's pattern mixed, printed p. 21, PDF p. 23); in DREAMS the cohort followed longest had the largest effect. Anchors outside the program: consumption gains about as large in year 3 as in year 2 in six countries (Banerjee et al. 2015) and growing to year 7 in Bangladesh (Bandiera et al. 2017), against Uganda's cash grants for trades, whose earnings gains were gone between year 4 and year 9 (Blattman, Fiala and Martinez 2020), a fast fade after year 4. 5% a year as the best guess: no fade seen so far, some later as the light package's businesses face competition; 0 to 20%. The trial's cohort comparison can't tell 5% from 10% a year; the choice rests on the outside anchors, most of which show gains holding for several years.

rows.label: Years the consumption gain lasts, counted from the program year
rows.explainer: How long the (fading) gain lasts before it stops. The core trial measured households 6 months to 2.5 years after the program (3.5 years after it started) and still found gains; DREAMS only to 18 months. Anchors: GiveWell's 2024 value-of-information estimate for Raising the Village, a similar livelihoods program in Uganda, counts its effects 3 years as a best guess, from a trial with one year of follow-up (models/grants/givewell/raising-the-village-2024); heavier graduation programs kept their consumption gains at least a year after implementation ended in six countries (Banerjee et al. 2015), 7 years in Bangladesh (Bandiera et al. 2017) and 10 years in India (Banerjee, Duflo and Sharma 2021); cash grants to start trades in Uganda raised earnings at 4 years but the controls caught up by year 9 (Blattman, Fiala and Martinez 2020). This program has more follow-up than Raising the Village's trial but a lighter package than BRAC's, so 8 years with the fade above (worth about 6 years of the full gain), 3 (what the trial saw) to 12.

rows.label: Present value of a yearly gain over its years, fading
rows.explainer: The years a yearly gain counts, fading by fade_rate each year and discounted at the shared rate, the first year in full.

rows.label: Core program (Kenya, Uganda, Rwanda): households times first-year ln gain
rows.formula: households_kenya * core_kenya_ln_gain_year + core_uganda_households * core_uganda_ln_gain_year + households_rwanda * core_rwanda_ln_gain_year
rows.explainer: Each core country's households times its yearly gain in ln(consumption), before adjustments; the branch's weight in the averages below.

rows.label: DREAMS Uganda: households times first-year ln gain
DREAMS Tanzania: households times first-year ln gain
DREAMS Ethiopia: households times first-year ln gain
SPRINT: households times first-year ln gain
rows.explainer: SPRINT takes the core trial's Ugandan effect, the same program in the same country, with its doubt about digital delivery in sprint_evidence_adj.

rows.label: Total ln(consumption) gain per person, present value
rows.formula: (core_ln_raw * core_evidence_adj * core_missing_data_adj + dreams_uganda_ln_raw * dreams_uganda_evidence_adj * dreams_uganda_missing_data_adj + dreams_tanzania_ln_raw * dreams_tanzania_evidence_adj * dreams_tanzania_missing_data_adj + dreams_ethiopia_ln_raw * dreams_ethiopia_evidence_adj * dreams_ethiopia_missing_data_adj + sprint_ln_raw * sprint_evidence_adj * sprint_missing_data_adj) / households * persistence_pv
rows.explainer: Each group's yearly gain (Kenya, Uganda and Rwanda from the core trial, DREAMS Uganda and Tanzania from the DREAMS trial, Ethiopia from its refugee subgroup), times its branch's evidence adjustment and missing-data step, weighted by its households, over the years it lasts, fading each year and discounted at the shared rate (the first year in full). A recurring income gain, as the template's explainer describes, not a one-off transfer: the seed grant is invested in the business, and the trials measure consumption from its returns.

rows.label: Spillover benefits to non-participants, as a share of participants' benefits
rows.explainer: Neither trial measured effects on non-participating neighbours: the impact-bond trial compared whole villages (so spillovers inside treated villages are invisible), and the DREAMS trial randomized households inside the same communities, where controls joined some savings groups and borrowed from participants (2% of control households joined a savings group, and some borrowed from participants: DREAMS report, PDF pp. 42-44), which if anything biases its effect down. Cash entering a village raises local incomes (Egger et al. 2022 for GiveDirectly's far larger transfers); Village Enterprise's transfers are a tenth of that size per household. 10% as the best guess, 0 to 40%. Business competition with non-participants is a negative share in unmodelled_benefits_adj.

rows.label: Mortality benefits as a share of consumption benefits
rows.explainer: Neither trial measured deaths, so 0, as the template asks for programs without mortality evidence; the high end allows for a child-mortality effect of a 6-18% consumption rise, much smaller than the effect GiveWell credits GiveDirectly's US$1,000 transfers with.

rows.label: Core program: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Measured (templates.md Convention 12): Village Enterprise's own published count of the entrepreneurs it trained in Kenya, Uganda and Rwanda meets two randomized trials of this program delivered by Village Enterprise's own mentors (IDinsight's development impact bond trial in Kenya and Uganda; Sedlmayr, Shah and Sulaiman's in Uganda). The SPRINT digital pilot is split out as its own thin branch. Rwanda has no trial of its own, but its households are trained and mentored by Village Enterprise's staff in the same program; the 14,500 government parasocial workers it trains (annual report p. 9) are the government-adoption row, not this count; how well the Kenyan and Ugandan effects carry to Rwanda is in core_evidence_adj. Nawiri's adapted package in northern Kenya added cash transfers, but Village Enterprise's grants in Nawiri were US$68,384 in all (Form 990 Part III), so the cash it paid is a negligible addition, left in the core consumption effect.

rows.label: DREAMS Uganda: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Measured: the charity's count of DREAMS households in Uganda meets IDinsight's household-level randomized trial of DREAMS itself, in the same settlements (Bidi Bidi and Rhino Camp).

rows.label: DREAMS Tanzania: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Thin: in Tanzania DREAMS is delivered by local community-based organisations that Village Enterprise trains, not by Village Enterprise and Mercy Corps, and no trial has tested that delivery; the effect is the Ugandan DREAMS trial's, carried over. The shared missing-data discount.

rows.label: DREAMS Ethiopia: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Measured: the charity's published count of the entrepreneurs it trained in the Dollo Ado camps (7,209) meets the DREAMS trial of the same program delivered the same way (Village Enterprise with Mercy Corps), in Uganda's refugee settlements; the effect's carry to Somali refugees in Ethiopia is in dreams_ethiopia_evidence_adj, not here.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, SPRINT digital delivery (internal and external validity)
rows.explainer: Internal validity 0.95, as core_evidence_adj, times a carry of about 0.8 to delivery by tablet and WhatsApp with five to ten times more entrepreneurs per mentor, which no trial has tested: lighter mentoring may lower the effect, though the training content and grants are the same. 0.75, 0.5 to 1; anchored on core_evidence_adj's 0.87, cut further for the untested channel.

rows.label: SPRINT: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Thin: digital delivery (tablets, WhatsApp mentoring) is other delivery than the in-person program the trials tested, and the reach is a judgment. The shared missing-data discount.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (internal and external validity), outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only
rows.formula: (core_ln_raw * core_evidence_adj + dreams_uganda_ln_raw * dreams_uganda_evidence_adj + dreams_tanzania_ln_raw * dreams_tanzania_evidence_adj + dreams_ethiopia_ln_raw * dreams_ethiopia_evidence_adj + sprint_ln_raw * sprint_evidence_adj) / (core_ln_raw + dreams_uganda_ln_raw + dreams_tanzania_ln_raw + dreams_ethiopia_ln_raw + sprint_ln_raw)
rows.explainer: The outcome-weighted average of the branch evidence adjustments (core_evidence_adj, dreams_uganda_evidence_adj, dreams_tanzania_evidence_adj, dreams_ethiopia_evidence_adj, sprint_evidence_adj), for reading only: each branch's own row is applied in ln_gain_per_person (Convention 4). After all adjustments the model credits about this × 0.95 × 0.98 of the trials' effects on participants, before shared credit and the wait.

rows.label: Missing-data step (outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only)
rows.formula: (core_ln_raw * core_evidence_adj * core_missing_data_adj + dreams_uganda_ln_raw * dreams_uganda_evidence_adj * dreams_uganda_missing_data_adj + dreams_tanzania_ln_raw * dreams_tanzania_evidence_adj * dreams_tanzania_missing_data_adj + dreams_ethiopia_ln_raw * dreams_ethiopia_evidence_adj * dreams_ethiopia_missing_data_adj + sprint_ln_raw * sprint_evidence_adj * sprint_missing_data_adj) / (core_ln_raw * core_evidence_adj + dreams_uganda_ln_raw * dreams_uganda_evidence_adj + dreams_tanzania_ln_raw * dreams_tanzania_evidence_adj + dreams_ethiopia_ln_raw * dreams_ethiopia_evidence_adj + sprint_ln_raw * sprint_evidence_adj)
rows.explainer: The outcome-weighted average of the branches' missing-data steps, for reading only: each branch's own step is applied in ln_gain_per_person (the government-adoption row applies its own). Tanzania's DREAMS and the SPRINT pilot are thin, so this sits a little below 1.

rows.label: Share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: The trials' effects are already net of their control groups, who got what they would have got anyway (food rations in the settlements, government transfers in Kenya). Below 1 only for government graduation programs (Kenya's KSEIP II, Rwanda's national graduation strategy) now expanding into the same areas, which may reach some households Village Enterprise enrols.

rows.label: Village Enterprise's DREAMS spending, FY2025

source.title: Village Enterprise Fund, Form 990 for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2025 (public disclosure copy)

rows.explainer: Village Enterprise's own DREAMS spending, including its US$2,323,287 subaward to Mercy Corps (Schedule I): the base for Mercy Corps' resources outside it.

rows.label: Mercy Corps' own DREAMS resources outside Village Enterprise's books, as a share of its DREAMS spending
rows.explainer: IDinsight's all-in DREAMS cost from both partners' data is US$540.95 per household (DREAMS report, section 5.3, PDF p. 77), against about US$548 from Village Enterprise's own books (its DREAMS spending with overhead over about 12,000 DREAMS households): so little of Mercy Corps' DREAMS work is paid outside the subaward. 5%, 0 to 20% for the market-systems work Mercy Corps may fund from other grants.

rows.label: Mercy Corps' own DREAMS resources
Government staff time helping target and deliver (Rwanda, Kenya)
rows.explainer: Rwanda's local officials and parasocial workers help target households and follow up (annual report p. 9), and Kenyan county and national staff work alongside the program. Unpublished: about 50 Rwandan officials giving a tenth of their time at about US$3,000 a year (US$15,000), about 50 Kenyan staff giving a tenth at about US$6,000 (US$30,000), and about 150 parasocial workers giving 200 hours a year to these households at about US$0.50 an hour (US$15,000), US$60,000, rounded up to US$80,000 for meetings and training not counted; 30,000 to 500,000.

rows.label: BOMA's own resources in Kuza Jamii (northern Kenya)
rows.explainer: BOMA leads the Kuza Jamii consortium in which Village Enterprise works in northern Kenya. Unpublished: Village Enterprise's Kuza Jamii work taken as about a third of its Kenyan spending (US$5.24M, so about US$1.7M), and BOMA's own management and delivery for those households as about 10% of that (5 to 15%): US$170,000, 50,000 to 500,000.

rows.label: Tanzanian community-based organisations' own delivery cost
rows.explainer: The local organisations deliver DREAMS to about 1,360 households after Village Enterprise trains them; their own staff and costs beyond what Village Enterprise pays are unpublished: about US$75 a household, US$100,000, 30,000 to 300,000.

rows.label: Entrepreneurs per savings group
rows.explainer: The program forms savings groups of about thirty entrepreneurs (the charity's description of the model); 25 to 35.

rows.label: Officers per savings group
rows.explainer: A chair, a treasurer and a secretary, the usual savings-group officers; 2 to 5.

rows.label: Each officer's unpaid hours a year beyond the meetings
rows.explainer: Record keeping, collecting and counting, about 1 to 2 hours a week beyond the meeting every member attends: 75 hours, 40 to 150.

rows.label: Hours in a working year
rows.explainer: The site's way of valuing a poor household's hour: a year's consumption over a 2,000-hour working year (as for time saved by water supply, facts/water.json). 1,500 to 2,500 for shorter or longer working years.

rows.label: Savings-group leaders' unpaid time, at the local wage
rows.explainer: Savings groups a year (households over members per group, about 1,600) × officers × their unpaid hours × an hour's value (consumption per person per year, the Kenyan control group's, over a working year: about US$0.19): about US$68,000.
rows.formula: households / sg_members_per_group * sg_officers_per_group * sg_officer_hours_per_year * baseline_consumption / hours_per_working_year

rows.label: Catholic Relief Services' and the Nawiri consortium's own resources for Village Enterprise's Nawiri households
rows.explainer: Nawiri's nutrition counselling and unconditional cash transfers came largely from Catholic Relief Services and the USAID consortium: Village Enterprise's own Nawiri spending was US$987,009, of which only US$68,384 in grants (Form 990 Part III). The partners' own spending on the same households, unpublished: about a third of Village Enterprise's, US$300,000, 100,000 to 1 million.

rows.label: Partners' resources outside Village Enterprise's cost
rows.formula: mercy_corps_own_usd + government_staff_usd + boma_usd + tanzania_cbo_usd + savings_leader_usd + crs_nawiri_usd

rows.label: This charity's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: Village Enterprise's share of all resources behind the outcome (Convention 2): its own cost over its cost plus each partner's resources valued above (Mercy Corps beyond its subaward, government staff, BOMA, Tanzania's community organisations, savings-group leaders' unpaid hours, Catholic Relief Services in Nawiri). About 0.96.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Share of reported households who get the program as studied
rows.explainer: The FY2025 count is Village Enterprise's own. In the impact-bond trial, 95.7% of households offered the program received at least the first grant, verified by IDinsight; 98% received the first grant in DREAMS. The effects used are on participants (treatment on the treated), so non-take-up is already out of them; this covers only counting error in the charity's own figure and the FY2025 households in programs cut short by the 2025 US stop-work order (Nawiri in northern Kenya and the USAID-funded Rwanda program, about 12% of program spending, some of whose households may have missed the second grant or mentoring; the annual report doesn't say how many), 0.98; and wastage, fraud and diversion of grants, 0.98 (GiveDirectly's model takes the same 2%). 0.96, 0.86 to 1.

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: Village Enterprise is funded by many private donors and foundations, and the loss of USAID funding in 2025 left gaps it had to fill (annual report p. 3), so little of a gift displaces other money; outcome funders and governments co-funding the model pull some in. 1, 0.85 to 1.1; the governments' wider adoption is uov_government_adoption, not here.

rows.label: Cash and investments held at the year's end

source.title: Village Enterprise Fund, Inc. and Affiliates, consolidated financial statements for the years ended June 30, 2025 and 2024 (audited, GRF CPAs & Advisors)

rows.explainer: Cash (US$5,080,971) plus investments (US$14,337,676) on 30 June 2025.

rows.label: Years a gift waits in funds held before it is spent
rows.explainer: Funds held over a year's spending, about 0.92 years: a gift joins the pool and is spent, on average, after that wait, as the site's other builds count it.

rows.label: Years from spending to the first consumption gains
rows.explainer: Each cohort's four months of targeting and training (audited statements, note 1) are spent before its first grant, and gains start soon after the grant; mentoring spending comes after the gains have started. The wait in funds held is gift_to_grant_years. The first grant comes about four months (0.33 years) after a cohort starts; 0.2 to 0.5.

rows.label: Discount for the wait until the gains start
rows.explainer: The wait in funds held and to the first gains, discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above; the evidence adjustments are applied per branch in ln_gain_per_person.

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Each effect not modelled, with its sign: assets still held after the consumption gain ends, net of depreciation (the businesses' assets are what produce the gain, so only what is left after persistence_years counts: core trial +US$40 assets per household, DREAMS +US$278 net assets, +US$184 household assets) +2% (0 to +3%); nutrition gains for malnourished children in the Nawiri program (6% of spending) beyond consumption +2% (0 to +5%); business competition with non-participating traders -2% (0 to -8%); savings groups for the Wildlife Conservation Society's farmers and fishers in Madagascar and the care-economy policy project in West Pokot, 0% (0 to +1%) together. Women's empowerment and wellbeing beyond consumption are valued through income only. Net +2%, the parts' ranges combined as independent: -5% to +7%. Governments adopting the model are uov_government_adoption; wastage and diversion of grants are in implementation_adj.

rows.label: Households a year reached by government graduation programs Village Enterprise helps
rows.explainer: Village Enterprise gives technical help to Rwanda's National Strategy for Sustainable Graduation (it is training 14,500 parasocial workers on its model and building the national management information system), three Kenyan counties adopting graduation frameworks, and Kenya's KSEIP, where the government delivered a cohort of 7,500 households itself, now KSEIP II with US$127M across 25 counties (annual report p. 9). No yearly count of households reached through these is published: anchored on KSEIP's 7,500-household government cohort and on Rwanda's parasocial workforce, if only a small share of its 14,500 workers each graduates a few households a year: 10,000, 3,000 to 60,000.

rows.label: Village Enterprise's share of the credit for those households
rows.explainer: The governments and the World Bank pay for the delivery and would run some graduation programs anyway; Village Enterprise's technical help is a small part of the cost and of the decision. 10%, 3 to 30%.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, government-delivered graduation
rows.explainer: The annual report cites an independent 2024 evaluation of KSEIP, the government-delivered version of this model, as having "increased household consumption by 30%" (p. 9), and a government-run graduation program in Niger had large effects in a trial (Bossuroy et al. 2022, Nature). Still cut: the KSEIP evaluation isn't public (its design and comparison group can't be checked), KSEIP's package included consumption support, and other governments' programs differ in mentoring intensity and targeting. 0.6, 0.3 to 0.9, below core_evidence_adj's 0.87 for Village Enterprise's own delivery.

rows.label: Government adoption: counted less where the outcome isn't measured
rows.explainer: Thin: neither the reach nor the effect of the governments' programs is measured for this charity. The shared missing-data discount.

rows.label: Units of value from governments adopting the model
rows.formula: gov_households_per_year * gov_credit_share * household_size * core_ln_raw / (households_kenya + core_uganda_households + households_rwanda) * persistence_pv * gov_evidence_adj * gov_missing_data_adj * $uov_per_ln_consumption * wait_discount
rows.explainer: Households reached through the governments × Village Enterprise's share of the credit × people per household × the core program's average yearly gain per household × the years it lasts × the evidence and missing-data steps, valued at the shared rate and after the same wait. One year's flow against one year's cost.
